newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT-T-bonds firm in face of US employment data.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-T-bonds firm in face of US employment data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury bond futures appear undeterred in their steep ascent one day before July U.S. employment statistics are released, some analysts said Thursday.
"People technically want to buy dips. I don't think one number is going to derail this rally right now," said Don Pullen, analyst with ED&F Man on the floor of the Chicago Board of Trade.
September bond futures put in another 1-1/2-year high at 116-31/32 Thursday, shaking off stronger-than-forecast second-quarter U.S. gross domestic product growth of 2.2 percent.
First-quarter GDP was revised down 1.0 percentage point to 4.9 percent, and the implicit price deflator, a key inflation measure, rose just 1.4 percent.
The contract overshot key resistance at 116-28/32 before pulling back to trade at moderately higher levels into the afternoon.
Pullen said his next upside target was 117-10/32 and saw support intraday at 116-17/32. A close above 116-00 would indicate the contract still has not put in a top, he said.
The 116-28/32 level is the high from December 1996 on continuation charts.

Stewart Taylor, president of Taylor Consulting, said prices approaching 117-00 will continue to pose a tough challenge for bond futures. The area "is very, very strong resistance, and the market arrived here in a very overbought condition," he said.
"When you rally 10 points off a low and do it in such a short amount of time, pullbacks can be kind of nasty."
Futures put in a low of 105-30/32 on April 11.
Taylor noted that related markets such as the dollar and commodities have been very kind to bonds, but that such favorable conditions generally don't last.
Still, Taylor said he was not ready to call a top in the market. "I'm not bearish," he said. "I just don't think the rally has a lot to go in the near term."
On the upside, floor traders are eyeing the 6.25 percent yield on the 30-year cash bond, which is roughly equivalent to 118-00 in September futures, Pullen said.

Bulls appear resolute despite talk that non-farm payrolls could now come in stronger than many analysts' original forecasts, Pullen said. According to a Reuters survey, the average estimate was 193,000.
Pullen said floor talk suggested the number could be as high as 240,000, based on a sharp drop in weekly state unemployment claims reported this morning and job ads data.
